subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Treponema pallidum is a slender, spiral-shaped spirochete that causes syphilis. It invades tissues, evades immunity, and spreads systemically, producing distinct clinical stages that guide diagnosis and treatment.

sections.p: Treponema pallidum is a motile, spiral bacterium that infects humans via mucosal or skin contact. It is highly adapted to survive in host tissues and evade immune detection, leading to a chronic, multi‑system disease.
The organism’s unique corkscrew motility and lack of a cell wall make it resistant to many antibiotics and difficult to culture. It relies on host enzymes for survival.
b: Requires blood or tissue for growth

t.b: Detects motile spirochetes in lesion exudate; positive confirms active infection
Screen for antibodies; positive indicates exposure but not necessarily active disease
Confirmatory treponemal tests; remain positive for life

sections.p: Transmission occurs through mucous membranes or broken skin during sexual contact or from mother to fetus. The bacterium survives in the host, disseminates via blood and lymph, and can remain latent.

t.b: Identifies source and prevents further spread; essential in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Syphilis progresses through primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages, each with characteristic manifestations. Early stages are most infectious and treatable.
Diagnosis integrates clinical presentation with serology and, when available, direct detection. In low‑resource settings, rapid tests and clinical judgment are key.

t.b: Screen for antibodies; high titers suggest active disease
Confirmatory; remains positive long after treatment
Detects DNA; useful when microscopy unavailable

sections.p: Penicillin remains the first‑line therapy because of its efficacy and safety. Alternatives are reserved for penicillin‑allergic patients and are less reliable.

t.b: Alternative when penicillin contraindicated; monitor for resistance

sections.p: Remember the classic painless chancre and the importance of serologic testing. In low‑resource settings, a positive non‑treponemal test followed by a confirmatory treponemal test is sufficient for treatment.
b: Primary chancre is painless, indurated, single
Non‑treponemal tests are screening, treponemal are confirmatory
Penicillin is the drug of choice

whenToSeekHelp: Neurosyphilis symptoms (confusion, vision loss), cardiovascular syphilis (heart failure), congenital syphilis (neonatal rash, hepatosplenomegaly)

faq.a: Yes, with appropriate penicillin therapy; early treatment prevents long‑term complications.

faq.q: Why is a painless ulcer a clue?
faq.a: Treponema pallidum causes a painless, indurated chancre, unlike many other genital ulcers.

faq.q: What if a patient has penicillin allergy?
faq.a: Use doxycycline or azithromycin, but monitor for treatment failure and consider desensitization if severe disease.

exam: Explain why a painless genital ulcer with a clean base suggests Treponema pallidum rather than Haemophilus ducreyi.
Describe the serologic testing algorithm for syphilis and interpret a scenario where VDRL is positive but FTA‑ABS is negative.
Outline the treatment regimen for a patient with secondary syphilis who is allergic to penicillin.
